title: What Is Base64 Encoding, Really?
excerpt: A plain-English explanation with a real example.
metaDescription: A plain-English explanation of Base64 encoding — what it actually does, why it exists, and when you'd use it, with real examples.
body:
Base64 shows up everywhere — email attachments, image data inside CSS files, API tokens — but it's often misunderstood as some kind of security feature. It isn't. It's a translation format, nothing more.

## What it actually does

Computers store data as binary — raw bytes that can include any value from 0–255. Some systems (older email protocols, JSON, URLs) were only built to safely carry plain text characters. Base64 solves that mismatch: it takes any binary data and re-represents it using only 64 safe characters — `A–Z`, `a–z`, `0–9`, `+`, and `/` — so it can travel through text-only systems without corruption.

## Why it exists

It groups the original data into 3-byte chunks and re-maps each chunk into 4 Base64 characters. That's also why Base64 output is always about 33% larger than the original — you're trading size for compatibility.

## A real example

The plain text `Hello` becomes this in Base64:

```
SGVsbG8=
```

The trailing `=` is padding — it appears when the input length doesn't divide evenly into those 3-byte chunks, so the last group needs filling out to stay a valid 4-character block.

## It is not encryption

Because Base64 is a defined, reversible mapping — not a secret — decoding it requires no password or key. If you paste that string into any Base64 decoder, you get `Hello` back immediately. Never use Base64 alone to "hide" sensitive information; it only obscures it from a casual glance.

faq.question: Is Base64 encryption?
faq.answer: No. Base64 is an encoding, not encryption — anyone can decode it instantly with no key or password, so it should never be relied on to protect sensitive data.

faq.question: Why does Base64 text end with = signs?
faq.answer: The = characters are padding, added when the original data length isn't a clean multiple of 3 bytes, so the encoded output lines up into complete 4-character groups.
